newsitem.title: CHINA: HK's Li Ka-shing, a classic rags to riches tale.
newsitem.headline: HK's Li Ka-shing, a classic rags to riches tale.

text.p: In Hong Kong business circles, Li Ka-shing is known as "superman" for his Midas touch.
He may be one of the world's richest men, but he claims he wears shoes with plastic soles because they last longer.
The 69-year-old business wizzard never fails to stun the market with surprise deals.

This week his flagship Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd and Whampoa Ltd Hutchison have made waves with news of a 3.03 percent stake in Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd and a 3.06 percent stake in Hongkong Land Holdings Ltd, pillars of the old British colonial order in Hong Kong.
An editorial in the South China Morning Post newspaper said Li's move could boost his Chinese patriotic credentials, coming just one month after China resumed sovereignty over Hong Kong.

Li Ka-shing's rise from rags to riches is a classic Hong Kong tale. Born in Chaozhou in south China, Li was among the tide of humanity to sweep south from China into the British colony where the streets were believed to be paved with gold.
They were for Li. Deprived of much of an education because he needed to work merely to survive, Li is Hong Kong's most prominent businessman.
Forbes magazine recently named him as the world's 15th richest individual, with net worth estimated at US$11 billion.
The tycoon has come a long way since his days assembling plastic flowers to put rice in his bowl.
He now controls a business empire spanning the globe in industries ranging from property, telecommunications, oil, electricity generation to container ports.
His flagships Cheung Kong and Hutchison are regarded as among the bluest of Hong Kong's blue chips.
The two together represent a market capitalisation of about HK$500 billion (US$64.60 billion).
Cheung Kong, along with several other blue-chip companies, made a raid on Hongkong Land in 1987.
After the October 1987 stock market crash the raiders sold the shares back to the Jardine group and made a gentlemen's agreement not to try another takeover for seven or eight years.

Li has not let his immense wealth go to his head. He lives a modest, ascestic life. He can be spotted walking the streets of the Central business district, often trailed by flocks of news-hungry reporters anxious to record every word he utters.
"My life is rather simple and I don't need much money," he said recently.

His wealth has endowed him with significant political clout. He was a member of China's Preparatory Committee responsible for hammering out the details of Hong Kong's reversion to China. The grouping has now been disbanded.
He was also an adviser to Beijing on Hong Kong affairs and a member of a committee that drafted Hong Kong's new constitution.
Li founded Cheung Kong, which turned out plastic trinkets, at the age of just 22, before beginning to dabble in property in the late 1950s.

Cheung Kong has ridden a property boom buoyed by Li's ability to spot a bargain and predict where the next upsurge would occur. One of his coups was to buy up land along what became Hong Kong's Mass Transit Railway.

He listed Cheung Kong in 1972, before acquiring Hutchison Whampoa Ltd a trading house and dockyard concern in 1979, quickly building it up into a diversified conglomerate operating in North America, Europe and Asia.

Li, a leading property developer, has time and again urged the administration to release more land for development, blaming soaring property prices on short supply rather than speculation which many see as a major cause for the spiral.
The tycoon is regarded as kingpin of his business empire, but he is gradually stepping back from the business world.
He is apparently handing over more and more company business to elder son Victor, letting him take a growing role to address news conferences while he himself takes a back seat.
News reports quote him as saying he wants to do "something meaningful." "I hope when I grow older, I will do more medical and education work," one report quoted Li as saying.
Widowed in 1990, Li has two sons, both Stanford-educated.

Victor, 33, is Cheung Kong's deputy chairman and deputy managing director. He is also an executive director of Hutchison. His brother Richard, 30, is Hutchison's deputy chairman. Richard also owns Singapore-based conglomerate Pacific Century Regional Developments Ltd.
